To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the binding sites of mAbs to the I domain of αLβ2 can be mapped to specific residues and that these residues can show large displacements, or small displacements, in response to lattice contact, or in response to affinity change at the ICAM- 1 binding site.
mAbs to the LFA-1 α I domain can competitively inhibit or allosterically inhibit binding to ligand, and can activate binding to ligand.

mAbs to the I domain of integrin αL bind to species-specific residues, and that the epitopes of mAbs that act as competitive antagonists are close to the ligand-binding site of the I domains, whereas the epitopes of allosteric antagonistic or agonistic mAbs are not.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how antibodies can inhibit, activate, and modulate the activity of the integrin I domain, which plays an essential role in the regulation of leukocyte adhesion.
the molecular basis for the action of mAbs that are either antagonistic or agonistic, and that can either compete for binding to the ligands or alter affinity for ligand through allosteric effects.

the molecular mechanisms by which antibodies to an integrin I domain affect the function of an intact heterodimer, and we have identified the binding sites and the molecular mechanisms by the mAbs that act by competitive inhibition, by allosteric inhibition, and by activation of ligand binding.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
competitive antagonists, allosteric antagonisms, and agonists all bind to the I domain of integrin αL, but in different locations.
the binding of mAbs to the I domains can be competitive or allosterically inhibitory or activating.
the I domain is a flexible molecule with a number of different binding sites for antibodies that can act as competitive or noncompetitive antagonists, or as agonists.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

mAbs that bind to regions of the I domain that are either close to the ligand or that show large displacements in response to lattice packing can act competitively or allosterically, while mAbs that bind distant from the ligands and that show little displacement can act as agonists.

mAbs to the integrin αI domain that bind to residues showing little conformational change can be agonists, whereas mAbs to residues that show large conformational change are more likely to be antagonists.

the α I domain has two binding sites for antibodies, one near the ligand binding pocket and one distant from it, which can be used to either competitively inhibit ligand binding or alter the conformation of the I domain.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a large number of binding sites on the integrin I domain that can be used to design mAbs that inhibit or activate integrins.
the I domain of the αL integrin subunit is a flexible structure that can undergo significant conformational changes in response to different lattice contacts.
mAbs that bind to the αL I domains of integrin LFA-1 can be classified into four groups based on their binding sites.
